title: 2 Kings 8:1–6
context: This episode returns to the Shunammite woman whose son Elisha had restored to life (4:8–37). The opening says Elisha “had spoken” to her, so the warning about a seven-year famine came earlier, and the text does not say exactly how this episode fits the chronology of the surrounding chapters. She lives among the Philistines for seven years, and on her return appeals to the king for her house and land. At that very moment Gehazi is telling the king about Elisha’s great deeds, including the raising of her son, and the king restores her property and its produce. Readers have noticed that Gehazi appears here in conversation with the king even though 5:27 ended with him leaving Elisha’s presence a leper; the text does not explain the timing, and this page does not speculate. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: God cares for the faithful woman through ordinary events and well-timed meetings.

verses.text: Now Elisha had spoken to the woman whose son he had restored to life, saying, “Arise, and go, you and your household, and stay for a while wherever you can; for the LORD has called for a famine. It will also come on the land for seven years.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha had warned the Shunammite woman of a seven-year famine and told her to go elsewhere. Arminian readers note that God’s warning gives her the opportunity to respond, and her obedience preserves her household. The verse shows God’s care for a woman who had shown hospitality to his prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD “has called for a famine,” stressing his rule over nature and history. Yet he also provides a warning and a refuge for his servant. Shared ground: both traditions see God’s sovereignty over the famine and his kindness toward the woman joined in this verse.

verses.text: The woman arose, and did according to the man of God’s word. She went with her household, and lived in the land of the Philistines for seven years.
verses.arminianNotes: The woman does according to the man of God’s word and lives among the Philistines for seven years. Arminian readers see trust expressed in costly obedience: she leaves her home and land on the strength of a prophetic word. Her response is a model of faith acting on what God has said.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see her obedience as the fruit of faith, and note that God preserves her even in a foreign land. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an example of trusting God’s word in practical decisions, with God caring for his people wherever they go.

verses.text: At the end of seven years, the woman returned from the land of the Philistines. Then she went out to beg the king for her house and for her land.
verses.arminianNotes: After seven years she returns and appeals to the king for her house and land. Arminian readers note that her obedience has left her without property, and she now acts boldly to seek justice. Faith does not make her passive; she takes responsible action to restore what was lost.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that her loss of land during her absence sets the stage for God’s provision through the king. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing a faithful woman seeking what is right, while the narrative prepares to show God’s care in the timing of her appeal.

verses.text: Now the king was talking with Gehazi the servant of the man of God, saying, “Please tell me all the great things that Elisha has done.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king is asking Gehazi to tell all the great things Elisha has done. Arminian readers note that even a king of Israel is curious about the prophet’s deeds. The conversation becomes the setting in which the woman’s appeal is heard, which shows God working through ordinary events.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the conversation as part of God’s providential arrangement: the story of the woman’s son is being told just as she arrives. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as preparing a striking coincidence that the narrative presents as God’s care, while the text does not explain the timing of Gehazi’s presence.

verses.text: As he was telling the king how he had restored to life him who was dead, behold, the woman whose son he had restored to life begged the king for her house and for her land. Gehazi said, “My lord, O king, this is the woman, and this is her son, whom Elisha restored to life.”
verses.arminianNotes: Just as Gehazi tells how Elisha restored a dead child to life, the woman arrives to make her appeal. Arminian readers note the remarkable timing, which they read as God’s gracious guidance of events in response to the woman’s faithful obedience. Gehazi identifies her and her son on the spot.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the timing as a clear instance of God’s providence ordering the smallest details for his people’s good. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing God’s hand in the meeting, and both affirm that God’s care for his people extends to the ordinary circumstances of their lives.

verses.text: When the king asked the woman, she told him. So the king appointed to her a certain officer, saying, “Restore all that was hers, and all the fruits of the field since the day that she left the land, even until now.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king hears the woman’s account and appoints an officer to restore all that was hers, including the produce of her fields. Arminian readers note the king’s just response and the full restoration. God’s care for the woman reaches through a human ruler’s willing decision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the restoration exceeds what she asked: not only her land but all its fruits since she left. God provides generously through the king. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as God vindicating a faithful woman through just human authority.
